concepts.name: Definition and Compositional Distinction: Core vs Headline Inflation
key_dimensions: Headline inflation includes all goods/services in the price index (food, fuel, and core); core inflation explicitly excludes food and energy components
Rationale for exclusion: food and energy prices are supply-shock driven and volatile, not reflective of demand-side pressures
Common UPSC trap: 'Core inflation is always lower than headline inflation' — this is FALSE; core can exceed headline during commodity price crashes
WPI vs CPI context: both have headline measures, but core derivation differs across indices

concepts.name: CPI-Based Headline Inflation: Structure and Weights
key_dimensions: CPI (Combined) is the official inflation benchmark for monetary policy in India since 2014
Weights: Food and Beverages (~45.86%), Fuel and Light (~6.84%), Miscellaneous (~28.32%) — food dominates, making CPI headline highly volatile
Base year revision: 2012=100 (current); implications of base year change on measured inflation
Rural vs Urban CPI: different weights assigned, leading to divergence in measured inflation across segments

concepts.name: WPI-Based Headline Inflation: Composition and Policy Relevance
key_dimensions: WPI measures wholesale price changes at the producer/trader level; base year 2011-12
Three major groups: Primary Articles (~22.6%), Fuel & Power (~13.1%), Manufactured Products (~64.2%)
WPI is no longer the primary policy anchor but remains relevant for deflating GDP and tracking supply-side inflation
UPSC trap: WPI does not include services; CPI does — this is a critical structural difference

concepts.name: Core Inflation Measurement in India: Methodological Variations
key_dimensions: India has no officially published 'core inflation' series; it is derived by excluding food and fuel from CPI — making it a computed, not a notified, measure
RBI uses 'CPI excluding food and fuel' as its operational proxy for core inflation
Alternative measures: 'trimmed mean inflation' and 'weighted median inflation' used globally but not standard in India
UPSC angle: absence of an official core inflation series means analysts may report different core figures — a deliberate examination trap

concepts.name: Role of Core Inflation in RBI's Monetary Policy Framework
key_dimensions: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework (2016): RBI mandated to keep CPI headline inflation at 4% ±2% — headline, NOT core, is the legal target
Yet RBI's MPC deliberations rely heavily on core inflation trends to assess demand-side pressures before changing repo rate
Persistent core inflation signals entrenched inflation expectations, prompting rate hikes even when headline is supply-driven
UPSC trap: students confuse the 'target' (headline CPI) with the 'diagnostic tool' (core inflation) — these are different roles

concepts.name: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) Framework and Inflation Band
key_dimensions: Established under amended RBI Act Section 45ZA; target set by Government of India in consultation with RBI every 5 years
Current target: 4% CPI with upper tolerance of 6% and lower tolerance of 2% (effective 2016, renewed 2021 for 2021-26)
Breach condition: if inflation remains outside 6% or below 2% for three consecutive quarters, RBI must report to government — a critical accountability mechanism
FIT uses headline CPI, not core: this is because food inflation directly impacts household welfare and inflation expectations in India

concepts.name: Food Inflation: Why It Dominates Indian Headline Inflation
key_dimensions: Food and beverages weight ~45.86% in CPI — among the highest weightage globally for a major economy; reflects consumption patterns of lower-income households
Structural drivers: monsoon dependency, MSP revisions, supply chain inefficiencies, vegetable price spikes (perishables like tomatoes, onions)
High food inflation creates 'base effect' distortions that can make headline appear to moderate even when underlying pressures persist
Policy tension: RBI cannot control food inflation through rate hikes (supply-side issue), yet it breaches the headline target — this is the core-headline policy dilemma

concepts.name: Fuel and Energy Inflation: The Second Excluded Component
key_dimensions: Fuel and Light weight in CPI (~6.84%); includes LPG, kerosene, firewood — not petrol/diesel directly in CPI fuel sub-index
Petrol and diesel are captured under 'Transport' in CPI Miscellaneous group — UPSC trap on where fuel prices actually appear in CPI
Energy price volatility is global and supply-driven (OPEC decisions, geopolitical events); monetary policy cannot address it, justifying exclusion from core
Administered vs market prices: India's partially administered fuel prices can suppress or amplify measured fuel inflation, distorting headline figures

concepts.name: Stagflation and the Core-Headline Divergence Problem
key_dimensions: Stagflation: simultaneous high inflation and low/negative growth — headline inflation rises (food/fuel shocks) while core inflation remains low or moderate
Policy dilemma: rate hikes to control headline stagflation damage growth further; rate cuts to boost growth worsen inflation
India's experience: 2011-13 period saw high headline CPI alongside slowing growth — classic core-headline divergence driven by food and fuel
Core inflation as the true barometer: low core during stagflation suggests demand is weak, rate hikes are counterproductive — a key MPC reasoning tool

concepts.name: Inflation Expectations and the Transmission from Headline to Core
key_dimensions: Persistent headline inflation (even if supply-driven) can de-anchor inflation expectations, causing wage-price spirals that eventually embed into core inflation
Second-round effects: high food prices → demand for higher wages → higher manufacturing costs → core inflation rises with a lag
RBI's Inflation Expectations Survey of Households: tracks 3-month and 1-year ahead expectations; used to assess whether headline-to-core transmission is occurring
UPSC angle: headline inflation is the 'trigger,' core inflation is the 'consequence' of unanchored expectations — this sequence is important for prelims and mains

concepts.name: GDP Deflator vs CPI vs WPI: Overlaps and Distinctions
key_dimensions: GDP Deflator = Nominal GDP / Real GDP × 100; broadest measure of economy-wide inflation, includes services not in WPI
GDP Deflator is not a 'cost of living' index; CPI is — this is the key functional distinction
WPI used for deflating manufacturing sector output in national accounts; GDP Deflator is the aggregate
UPSC trap: 'Which is the most comprehensive inflation measure?' — GDP Deflator, not CPI or WPI, because it covers the entire economy

concepts.name: Base Effect in Inflation Measurement
key_dimensions: Base effect: a high price level in the base year makes current inflation appear lower (favorable base effect) and vice versa
Critically affects headline more than core: food and fuel prices are more volatile, creating stronger base effects in headline CPI
RBI explicitly adjusts for base effects in MPC statements when interpreting monthly inflation data
UPSC trap: a 'fall in inflation' due to base effect does NOT mean prices fell — only the rate of increase slowed; price level can still be rising

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Transmission: Why Core Inflation is More Rate-Sensitive
key_dimensions: Core inflation (manufactured goods, services) is driven by demand-side factors — credit growth, consumption spending — which are directly influenced by interest rates
Food and fuel inflation are supply-determined; raising repo rate does not reduce tomato prices or crude oil prices
Transmission channels: repo rate → bank lending rates → credit demand → consumption/investment → demand-pull core inflation
Implication for UPSC mains: when RBI hikes rates to 'control inflation,' it is operationally targeting core inflation mechanisms, even though the legal mandate is headline CPI

concepts.name: Producer Price Index (PPI) vs WPI: The Unrealized Transition
key_dimensions: India uses WPI as producer-level price index; globally, PPI is standard (used by USA, EU) — India has been deliberating PPI adoption since 2014 Urjit Patel Committee
WPI measures prices at the wholesale/first point of sale; PPI measures prices from the producer's perspective, excluding trade margins
PPI would give a cleaner measure of supply-side inflationary pressure, separating production cost inflation from distribution inflation
UPSC relevance: committee recommendations for PPI adoption appear in economic surveys; question on 'why India should shift from WPI to PPI' is a recurring mains theme

concepts.name: Disinflation vs Deflation vs Negative Inflation: Conceptual Traps
key_dimensions: Disinflation: inflation rate is falling but still positive (e.g., from 6% to 3%) — prices still rising, just slower
Deflation: general price level is falling (negative inflation rate) — associated with demand collapse, debt deflation spiral
India experienced WPI deflation in 2015-16 (negative WPI) while CPI remained positive — highlights index-level divergence
UPSC trap: 'WPI deflation means prices fell for consumers' — FALSE; CPI remained above 4% during the same period, showing core-headline and WPI-CPI simultaneous divergence

concepts.name: Suppressed Inflation and Administered Prices in India
key_dimensions: Suppressed inflation: government-controlled prices (fuel, fertilizers, electricity) keep measured inflation artificially low; when decontrolled, inflation surges
India's fuel price deregulation (petrol in 2010, diesel in 2014) caused a one-time headline inflation spike — this is 'price level adjustment,' not structural inflation
Administered prices affect headline inflation directly but may not affect core inflation if they don't trigger second-round wage-price effects
MSP for agricultural commodities: upward MSP revisions directly feed into food inflation component of headline CPI — a deliberate policy-inflation linkage UPSC tests

concepts.name: K-Core and Trimmed Mean: Alternative Core Inflation Measures
key_dimensions: Trimmed mean inflation: excludes a fixed percentage of items with the highest and lowest price changes each period — captures a dynamic 'core' rather than fixed exclusion
K-core: excludes the top and bottom K% of items by price change magnitude; more robust than simple food-fuel exclusion
These measures are used in academic RBI research papers and have appeared in Economic Survey discussions — relevant for advanced mains answers
UPSC angle: question on 'limitations of conventional core inflation measurement' requires knowledge of these alternatives to score differentiated marks

concepts.name: Global Commodity Prices and Import-Driven (Cost-Push) Headline Inflation
key_dimensions: India is a net importer of crude oil, edible oils, and pulses — global price shocks directly transmit to domestic headline inflation through import channel
Exchange rate depreciation amplifies import inflation: rupee weakening → higher import costs → higher fuel and commodity prices → headline CPI rises
This is 'imported inflation' — beyond RBI's direct control, yet it breaches headline targets, creating accountability pressure under FIT
Core inflation remains insulated from short-term commodity shocks but can be affected if import costs persist and feed into manufactured goods prices over time

concepts.name: Urjit Patel Committee Recommendations (2014): Institutionalizing Headline CPI as Target
key_dimensions: Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework (2014) — chaired by Urjit Patel; recommended CPI as nominal anchor over WPI
Recommended glide path: CPI below 8% by Jan 2015, below 6% by Jan 2016, 4% ±2% thereafter — which was institutionalized in the 2016 FIT framework
Committee explicitly chose headline CPI (not core) because food inflation directly affects the poor and influences inflation expectations in India's context
UPSC trap: students attribute FIT solely to RBI Act amendment — but the intellectual foundation was the Urjit Patel Committee; both are needed for complete answers

concepts.name: Core Inflation Stickiness and Its Implications for Rate Cut Decisions
key_dimensions: Core inflation is 'sticky' — it does not fall as quickly as headline inflation because services pricing (rentals, education, healthcare) adjusts slowly downward
Post-COVID India: headline CPI moderated due to base effects and food price correction, but core inflation remained elevated (~5-6%), preventing aggressive rate cuts
RBI's communication challenge: explaining why rates remain high when headline appears benign — answer lies in sticky core inflation
UPSC mains question pattern: 'Despite headline inflation moderating, RBI maintained repo rate. Analyze.' — requires core inflation stickiness as central argument
